name: Model Liability and Errors and Omissions

Algorithmic bias class actions in hiring, lending and tenant screening, autonomous agents executing bad transactions, diagnostic AI malpractice, hallucinated professional advice, autonomous vehicle product liability, trading bot losses, industrial control misconfiguration, chatbot defamation and unauthorised commitments, coding assistant vulnerabilities, and deepfake wire fraud.

reading.body:
Ten distinct liability categories now make up AI errors and omissions exposure, from algorithmic bias class actions to deepfake wire fraud.

The categories span hiring, lending, healthcare, driving, trading, industrial operations, customer service, software development, and fraud. That breadth means a single model can create liability in multiple unrelated domains, and a single enterprise may need coverage across several of them.

A recurring shift appears across these categories. Autonomous vehicle liability moves from driver to software developer, diagnostic errors attach to health systems and developers, and chatbot commitments bind the operator. As AI takes actions rather than advising, errors and omissions risk becomes a product liability problem, not just a professional negligence problem.

What is absent is frequency, severity, or cost. The list gives no claim counts, payout amounts, or premium trends, and it does not say which category is most likely or most expensive. It is a taxonomy of exposure, not a measure of risk.

The ten categories are not ten separate risks. They are ten places where the same transfer of liability lands: from the person who acted to the party that supplied the model. Autonomous vehicle liability moving from driver to developer is the clearest case, but diagnostic AI malpractice attaching to health systems and developers, chatbot commitments binding the operator, and coding assistant vulnerabilities exposing the tool vendor all describe the same movement. The taxonomy is a list of counterparties, not a list of technologies.

That transfer explains why the categories cluster around actions rather than advice. Where a model only recommends, the professional who accepted the recommendation still carries the negligence. Where a model executes, corrupts, transfers, adjusts, or issues, there is no human act to attach the claim to, so it attaches to the system. Autonomous agent execution failures, trading bot flash crashes, industrial control misconfiguration, and deepfake wire fraud all sit on the execution side of that line.

The practical consequence is that coverage has to be assembled per deployment, not per model. A single model used in hiring, in customer service, and inside a coding assistant generates exposure in three categories with three different counterparties and three different policy triggers. Nothing in the data says how those triggers interact, whether one policy responds to all three, or where the boundaries between them fall.

Which AI liability category is most likely to produce a claim?
The data does not hold this. It lists ten categories with no claim counts, frequencies, or severity, so no ranking is possible from what is given.

What is the difference between AI errors and omissions and AI product liability?
The data does not draw that distinction explicitly. It shows liability shifting toward the party that supplied or operates the model in several categories, including autonomous vehicles, diagnostic tools, and chatbots, which is the direction product liability would point.

Does one insurance policy cover all ten categories?
The data does not say. It presents ten distinct categories with separate source pages, which implies separate treatment, but no policy structure, limits, or exclusions appear in the data.

Which categories involve a model taking an action rather than giving advice?
Autonomous agent execution failures, trading bot flash crashes, industrial control misconfiguration, and deepfake wire fraud all describe a model or synthesised media causing a transaction or physical adjustment. Diagnostic AI malpractice and autonomous vehicle product liability involve a model acting in a clinical or driving decision.

Who is the defendant in an algorithmic bias class action?
The data names the claim type and the domains, hiring, mortgage processing, tenant screening, and healthcare, but does not identify which party is sued. It does not distinguish employer, lender, landlord, or vendor.

How often does the list of categories change?
The data gives a refresh interval of 30 days and a build date of 2026-09-15, so the page is rebuilt monthly. It does not indicate whether the ten categories themselves are expected to change at that interval.
